questions.question: 1. Which one of the following data structures is used in DFS?

explanations.a: Incorrect. A heap is not the standard data structure used to control the traversal order in DFS.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A deque can be used in some algorithms, but it is not the standard structure associated with DFS.
explanations.c: Incorrect. DFS does not select vertices according to priority.
explanations.d: Correct. DFS uses a stack in its iterative implementation; recursion also relies on the call stack.

answers.a: Going to the parent or an earlier vertex when all reachable choices from the current path have been explored
answers.b: Going to the parent node whenever any child node has been visited
answers.c: Going to a sibling node immediately after visiting one child
answers.d: Going to a sibling node before visiting the current vertex

explanations.a: Correct. DFS backtracks to an earlier vertex when the current path cannot be extended through an unvisited adjacent vertex.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Visiting one child does not by itself cause DFS to backtrack.
explanations.c: Incorrect. DFS does not necessarily move directly to a sibling after visiting one child; it first continues as deeply as possible.
explanations.d: Incorrect. DFS visits the current vertex before exploring its adjacent vertices.

questions.question: 3. What should DFS do when it encounters an already visited vertex?

answers.b: Ignore that vertex for the current traversal step and continue with another unvisited option if available.
answers.c: Delete the vertex from the graph.
answers.d: Restart the entire DFS from the source.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Repeatedly processing an already visited vertex can cause unnecessary revisits and may lead to cycles in the traversal process.
explanations.b: Correct. DFS uses the visited status to avoid processing the same vertex again and continues with another unvisited adjacent vertex when possible.
explanations.c: Incorrect. DFS does not modify the graph by deleting vertices.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Encountering a visited vertex does not require restarting the traversal.

questions.question: 4. Which statement correctly describes recursive DFS?

answers.a: It requires a queue to store all vertices before traversal begins.
answers.b: It visits only vertices having exactly one neighbor.
answers.c: It uses recursive function calls, with the call stack supporting the depth-first traversal and backtracking.
answers.d: It cannot be applied to graphs containing cycles.

explanations.a: Incorrect. A queue is not the defining structure for recursive DFS.
explanations.b: Incorrect. DFS can visit vertices with any number of adjacent vertices.
explanations.c: Correct. Recursive DFS uses function calls to move deeper into the graph, while the call stack preserves the state needed for backtracking.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Recursive DFS can be applied to cyclic graphs when visited information is maintained.

questions.question: 5. In DFS, why is a visited array or set maintained?

answers.a: To store the numerical value of every edge
answers.b: To determine the weight of each vertex
answers.d: To prevent a vertex from being processed repeatedly

explanations.a: Incorrect. A visited array or set records traversal status rather than edge values.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Visited information does not represent vertex weights.
explanations.c: Incorrect. DFS does not use the visited structure to sort vertices.
explanations.d: Correct. Marking vertices as visited prevents DFS from repeatedly processing the same vertex.

questions.question: 6. Which of the following can DFS be used for?

answers.b: Finding the average value of all vertex labels
answers.c: Changing all directed edges into undirected edges
answers.d: Automatically assigning numerical labels to all vertices

explanations.a: Correct. DFS can be used to explore all vertices reachable from a starting vertex and thereby identify connected components.
explanations.b: Incorrect. DFS may visit vertex labels, but computing their average is not a specific application of DFS.
explanations.c: Incorrect. DFS does not modify the direction of edges.
explanations.d: Incorrect. DFS can assign traversal information, but automatically assigning arbitrary numerical labels is not its purpose.

questions.question: 7. Which of the following best describes the DFS traversal of a graph with cycles?

answers.a: DFS must stop immediately when it encounters any edge that forms a cycle.
answers.b: DFS can continue correctly by using visited information to avoid repeatedly processing vertices.
answers.c: DFS cannot be applied to a cyclic graph.
answers.d: DFS removes every cyclic edge before continuing.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Encountering an edge associated with a cycle does not necessarily terminate the entire DFS traversal.
explanations.b: Correct. A visited structure allows DFS to handle cyclic graphs without repeatedly processing the same vertices.
explanations.c: Incorrect. DFS is applicable to both cyclic and acyclic graphs.
explanations.d: Incorrect. DFS traverses the graph without removing edges.

questions.question: 8. Suppose DFS starts at vertex $A$ and follows the path $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C$. Vertex $C$ has no unvisited adjacent vertex. What should happen next?

answers.b: DFS starts again from $A$ without returning through the current path.
answers.c: DFS backtracks from $C$ to an earlier vertex such as $B$ to look for another unvisited path.
answers.d: DFS converts the path into a queue.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Reaching a vertex with no unvisited neighbor does not cause DFS to delete it.
explanations.b: Incorrect. DFS uses the existing traversal state and backtracks rather than restarting unnecessarily.
explanations.c: Correct. When $C$ cannot be explored further, DFS backtracks to an earlier vertex and checks whether another unvisited adjacent vertex is available.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A traversal path is not converted into a queue when DFS backtracks.

questions.question: 9. If an iterative DFS uses a stack, which vertex is processed first when several vertices are available on the stack?

answers.a: The vertex most recently pushed onto the stack
answers.b: The vertex that was pushed first
answers.c: The vertex with the smallest label
answers.d: The vertex with the largest label

explanations.a: Correct. A stack follows the LIFO principle, so the most recently pushed vertex is the next one removed for processing.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Processing the first pushed vertex would follow FIFO behavior rather than the usual stack behavior.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A stack does not select its next element based on numerical labels.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A stack does not select its next element based on the largest numerical label.
